## About metformin
Metformin is a medicine used to treat type 2 diabetes. It helps to lower blood sugar by making the body respond better to its own insulin.

## How and when to take it
Metformin tablets are usually taken with or just after a meal. Taking the tablet with food helps to reduce stomach upset such as feeling sick, which is most common in the first weeks of treatment. Swallow the tablet whole with a glass of water and do not crush or chew it unless the leaflet in your pack says you can.

Most people take metformin two or three times a day, for example with breakfast and with the evening meal. The exact dose depends on your blood sugar levels and on how well your kidneys work, so your doctor will tell you how many to take. Always follow the label on your pack rather than a dose you read somewhere else.

Some people are given slow release metformin, which is taken once a day with the evening meal. Slow release tablets must be swallowed whole. You may notice something that looks like a tablet shell in your stool. This is normal because the medicine has already been absorbed.

Your doctor or pharmacist may check your kidneys with a blood test before you start and from time to time afterwards, because metformin is cleared from the body by the kidneys. Tell them if you are being sick, have diarrhoea or cannot drink enough, as they may ask you to pause the tablets until you are well again. Keep your regular diabetes appointments and bring your tablets with you.

Tell them if you are being sick, have diarrhoea or cannot drink enough, as they may ask you to pause the tablets until you are well again. Keep your regular diabetes appointments and bring your tablets with you.

If you forget a dose, take it as soon as you remember, but only if it is with food. If it is nearly time for your next dose, skip the missed one. Never take a double dose to make up for a forgotten one. Keep taking metformin even when you feel well, and talk to your doctor before you stop.

## Side effects
Common side effects of metformin include feeling sick, diarrhoea, stomach pain and a metallic taste in the mouth. These often improve after the first few weeks. Taking the tablets with food can help.

Tell your doctor if you feel very tired, have muscle pain or breathe fast, as these can be signs of a rare but serious problem.

## Alcohol
Drinking a lot of alcohol while taking metformin raises the chance of a rare problem called lactic acidosis. Try to stay within the usual low risk limits.
